output.summary: KEP-2232 proposed letting users suspend and resume Jobs, which deletes active Pods and stops the Job controller from creating new ones until resumed, and allows creating Jobs in a suspended state. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
output.rationale: Users needed to pause a Job mid-execution, but the only workaround was deleting and re-creating the Job, which loses metadata such as the list of successful/failed Pods and logs. The design adds a suspend flag so Pod creation can be delayed indefinitely and resumed later. The KEP chose a native Kubernetes feature over an external controller using an orchestratorName field, which the document judged to add unnecessary complexity and make Job ownership hard to track.

alternatives.option: Delete and re-create the Job to pause it
alternatives.why_not: Deletes Job metadata such as the list of successful/failed Pods and logs, as the motivation section states.

alternatives.option: External controller using an orchestratorName field so the default Job controller ignores the Job
alternatives.why_not: The document says it adds unnecessary complexity and the need for additional control plane components, and makes ownership of the Job hard to track.

evidence.quote: Suspending a Job will delete all active Pods owned by that Job and also instruct the controller manager to not create new Pods until the Job is resumed.
as a workaround, users can delete and re-create the Job, but this will also delete Job metadata such as the list of successful/failed Pods and logs.
While this approach is similar to the `schedulerName` field used in kube-scheduler, it adds unnecessary complexity and the need for additional control plane components to handle Jobs.
In addition, this approach makes ownership of the Job hard to track.
